item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Rightmove posts 10-year high in agent retention as revenue climbs
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rightmove has reported its strongest estate agent retention rates in over a decade alongside rising revenues, as the property portal continues to expand its AI-powered tools for the industry. The platform saw a 9% increase in agency revenue during the first half of 2026, driven by more agents upgrading to premium packages and adopting additional services.

Technology driving growth

The property portal attributed part of its success to significant investment in artificial intelligence, with 46 AI initiatives currently in development. Rightmove's automated valuation tool reportedly generated 50% more valuation leads for agents, while its new conversational search feature "Ask Rightmove" increased user engagement by approximately 40%. The company launched 40% more tech products and enhancements compared to the same period last year, with additional AI-powered workflow tools for agents expected later in 2026.

Johan Svanstrom, Rightmove's CEO, commented: "Our investment in agent-focused solutions is delivering results, building on strong foundations laid in recent years. Early indicators show our conversational search feature nearly doubles the likelihood of users sending enquiries to agents."

Market challenges remain

Despite positive performance in its core agency business, Rightmove has revised its full-year revenue growth forecast downwards to 6-8%, from an initial 8-10% projection. This adjustment reflects ongoing challenges in the new-build sector, where development listings fell by 6% year-on-year. The company maintained its profit guidance, citing effective cost management.

Rightmove also announced plans to return over £400m to shareholders in the coming year, including approximately £330m through an expanded share buyback programme. This will be funded through existing cash reserves and a new £200m credit facility.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, these developments suggest Rightmove is continuing to enhance its platform with more sophisticated property search tools. Estate agents may find the portal's growing suite of AI-powered products helps streamline operations and generate higher quality leads, though some might need to budget for potential package upgrades to access the full range of features.

item.title: Is a Burnham bounce emerging in the housing market?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market appears to be showing tentative signs of stabilisation after several months of subdued activity, with July's figures revealing a narrowing gap in agreed sales compared to 2025 levels. While the market had been running approximately 10% behind last year's pace since Easter, this shortfall reduced to 5.2% last month. Net sales figures, which account for collapsed transactions, have also shown unexpected resilience during what's typically a slower summer period.

Mixed signals across regions

Regional performance paints a varied picture when comparing current activity against different benchmark years. Scotland emerged as the only region to record annual growth, with sales up 0.3% compared to July 2025 and 15.7% higher than 2023 levels. The East of England showed the most significant three-year improvement, with transactions down just 2.7% from 2025 but up 21.1% from 2023.

London continues to trail other regions, with sales 4.4% lower than 2025 and only 5.6% ahead of 2023 figures. The North West experienced the sharpest annual decline at 9.5% below 2025 levels, though activity remains substantially higher than during the challenging market conditions of 2023.

Listing levels hold steady

New property listings have remained consistent with recent patterns, with 33,600 homes coming to market in week 29 - nearly identical to the previous week's 33,800. While this sits below the 2026 weekly average of 36,900, it aligns closely with the ten-year average for this period. Year-to-date figures show 1.069 million new listings, matching 2025's total and running 4.1% ahead of 2024's pace.

Completed sales figures tell a similar story of gradual improvement, with 24,000 homes sold subject to contract in week 29 - slightly above the previous week's 23,600 and close to the ten-year average of 24,800 for this period. The 2026 weekly average currently stands at 24,700 transactions.

Market observers continue to debate whether these improvements represent the beginning of a sustained recovery or simply reflect seasonal variations and temporary factors. With regional disparities remaining pronounced and economic uncertainties persisting, borrowers might consider monitoring local market conditions closely when planning their next property move.

item.title: Estate agents face longest wait on record to get paid
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Estate agents across Britain are facing unprecedented delays in receiving their fees, with the average property sale now taking over seven months from listing to completion, according to new Rightmove data. The property portal reveals transactions currently average 216 days nationally – the longest wait recorded at this time of year since records began.

Regional variations in completion times

The research highlights significant regional disparities in transaction speeds. London remains the slowest market, with agreed sales taking 174 days to complete on average – 33 days longer than the North East (141 days). Scotland maintains its position as the fastest-moving region at just 98 days, benefiting from its distinct legal system and more comprehensive upfront property information.

Property type also influences completion times, with flats proving the slowest at 169 days compared to 149 days for terraced and semi-detached homes. These extended timelines represent a 36-day increase since 2019, despite technological advancements in the property sector.

Challenges in the transaction process

Several factors continue to slow the home-moving process, including:

  • High conveyancing workloads across the country
  • Increasingly lengthy property chains
  • Complexities surrounding leasehold properties
  • Persistent manual processes in parts of the system

For estate agents, these delays create financial uncertainty, with sales remaining in limbo for months after being agreed. Rightmove's data shows approximately 24% of agreed sales initially fall through, while 6% collapse completely without returning to market within a year. The portal currently lists £205bn worth of residential property that must still navigate the completion process after finding buyers.

Rightmove has expressed support for proposed government reforms aimed at streamlining transactions, including earlier information sharing and greater conveyancing digitisation. The company argues these measures could reduce failed sales, improve certainty for all parties, and help agents convert agreed sales into completed deals more efficiently.

Johan Svanstrom, Rightmove's CEO, commented: "The current average 154-day wait between sale agreement and completion is simply unsustainable. A healthy housing market requires smoother, more predictable transactions that give buyers and sellers greater confidence in the process."

item.title: Bogus mortgage adviser sentenced over £203,000 fraud
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A fraudulent mortgage adviser who swindled over £200,000 from four victims has received a suspended prison sentence after admitting to multiple counts of fraud. The case highlights the importance of verifying financial advisers' credentials before entrusting them with sensitive transactions.

Deceptive mortgage scheme uncovered

Adam Francis, 48, from Banton, operated under the alias "The Mortgage Man" between 2017 and 2018, falsely presenting himself as a qualified financial adviser. Working with an accountant who has since passed away, Francis convinced victims he could secure mortgages for them, collecting deposits and fees that were never used for their intended purpose.

The fraudster maintained the illusion by engaging with legitimate professionals in the property sector, including estate agents and solicitors. He paid some initial fees to obtain authentic-looking documents, which he then showed to victims to suggest their applications were progressing. The scheme collapsed when victims contacted solicitors directly and discovered no funds had been deposited in client accounts.

Legal consequences and warning to borrowers

At Chester Crown Court, Francis received a 25-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, along with a rehabilitation order. The court heard how four victims lost a combined £203,436 in the scam. Detectives noted that none of the stolen money has been recovered.

Detective Constable Catrin Phoenix of Cheshire Police's Economic Crime Unit described Francis as "a cunning and deceitful individual" who exploited victims' trust. She emphasised that Francis lacked any legitimate financial qualifications and used the stolen funds for personal gain.

This case serves as a stark reminder for anyone seeking mortgage advice to:

  • Check the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) register to verify an adviser's credentials
  • Be wary of requests for large upfront payments
  • Confirm directly with solicitors about fund handling
  • Question any professional who avoids providing clear documentation

Whilst the suspended sentence brings some closure, the financial impact on victims remains significant. Borrowers might consider this case as motivation to exercise extra diligence when engaging financial services professionals.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest Nationwide house price data
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market showed signs of continued moderation in July, with Nationwide's latest figures revealing a slight slowdown in annual price growth. Property values increased by 1.8% compared to July 2023, down from June's 2.2% annual rise, while monthly growth remained virtually flat at just 0.1% after seasonal adjustments.

Economic headwinds persist

Analysts suggest several factors are contributing to the subdued market conditions. Ongoing geopolitical tensions, particularly in the Middle East, have introduced fresh volatility to energy markets and financial systems. This uncertainty appears to be weighing on buyer sentiment, with many households adopting a cautious approach amidst fluctuating interest rate expectations.

However, some positive indicators are emerging. The recent easing of inflationary pressures and moderating wage growth could provide the Bank of England with more flexibility in its monetary policy decisions. These developments may help stabilise mortgage rates in the coming months, potentially supporting market activity.

Tenure trends reveal housing mobility patterns

Nationwide's analysis of housing tenure reveals striking differences in how long households typically remain in their properties:

  • Outright homeowners stay longest, averaging nearly 24 years in the same property
  • Around 30% of outright owners have lived in their home for three decades or more
  • Private renters move most frequently, averaging five years per tenancy
  • Approximately half of private tenants relocate within two years

The data also shows that the majority of housing moves (around 75%) occur within the same tenure rather than between different housing sectors. The private rented sector accounts for the largest share of internal mobility, while approximately 200,000 households transitioned from renting to homeownership in the latest reporting period.

Industry perspective on market conditions

Propertymark CEO Nathan Emerson commented: "The housing market continues to demonstrate resilience despite economic uncertainties. While national figures suggest stability, we're seeing significant regional variations beneath the surface."

Emerson highlighted several key factors influencing current conditions, including constrained housing supply, fluctuating borrowing costs and uneven buyer demand across different locations. The recent Bank of England decision to maintain interest rates has provided some welcome stability for borrowers, allowing prospective buyers to make more informed decisions about their property purchases.

The combination of these factors suggests the housing market is likely to remain relatively subdued in the coming months. Homeowners considering a move may wish to monitor local market conditions closely, as regional variations continue to play an important role in property values and transaction volumes across the UK.

item.title: EYE NEWS UPDATE: Property industry reacts to Bank of England’s interest rate decision
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Bank of England has maintained interest rates at 3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting, offering temporary stability to mortgage borrowers amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. While three Monetary Policy Committee members voted for an increase to 4%, the majority opted to hold, with markets now scrutinising updated inflation forecasts for clues about future rate movements.

Mixed Economic Signals Influence Decision

Recent economic indicators presented a complex picture for policymakers. June's inflation rate eased to 2.6%, while wage growth slowed and unemployment remained stable – factors reducing immediate pressure for rate hikes. However, rising oil prices due to Middle East tensions have raised concerns about prolonged inflationary pressure, potentially affecting the Bank's future decisions.

The property market had largely anticipated this decision, with many lenders adjusting mortgage rates in advance. Industry experts suggest the MPC's cautious stance reflects balancing act between controlling inflation and supporting economic growth, particularly in the housing sector which remains sensitive to borrowing costs.

Property Market Reacts to Rate Stability

For homeowners and prospective buyers, the rate pause provides welcome breathing space after months of elevated mortgage costs. However, estate agents report the market remains finely balanced:

  • Asking prices are adjusting after initial over-valuation, with sensible offers being accepted
  • Inventory levels exceed buyer demand in many areas, creating a buyer's market
  • Some homeowners are choosing not to sell rather than accept lower prices

The standoff between buyers and sellers continues, with neither side willing to make significant concessions in many cases. Market participants suggest current conditions may persist until either mortgage rates fall significantly or economic confidence improves substantially.

Looking Ahead: What This Means for Borrowers

While the immediate rate freeze offers stability, borrowers might consider:

  • Reviewing fixed-rate deals before potential autumn rate adjustments
  • Monitoring lender pricing which may change independently of Bank Rate
  • Seeking independent mortgage advice to navigate the current climate

The Bank's next moves will depend heavily on inflation trends and global economic developments. With oil prices and geopolitical tensions adding uncertainty, borrowers may wish to prepare for potential rate volatility in coming months.

As the property market adjusts to this extended period of higher borrowing costs, both buyers and sellers appear to be adopting a cautious approach, with transaction volumes remaining below historical averages. The coming months will reveal whether this stability encourages more market activity or simply prolongs the current standoff.

item.title: The Guild offers members free webinar today to prepare for Phase Two of RRA
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Renters’ Rights Act continues to reshape the UK’s private rented sector, with Phase Two of the legislation set to introduce further reforms later this year. To help property professionals navigate these changes, The Guild of Property Professionals is hosting a dedicated webinar aimed at equipping members with the latest guidance.

Understanding the Renters’ Rights Act

Phase One of the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect on 1 May, brought significant changes to the rental market. Key measures included the conversion of assured shorthold tenancies into assured periodic tenancies, the abolition of Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions, and the introduction of reformed grounds for possession. These reforms aim to create a more transparent and accountable private rented sector.

Attention is now turning to Phase Two, which is expected to introduce a new database for the private rented sector. While this phase may involve fewer immediate operational changes, understanding the new requirements remains crucial for property agents and landlords alike.

Supporting Property Professionals

The Guild of Property Professionals is committed to helping its members stay informed and compliant with evolving legislation. On Thursday 30 July, the organisation will host a webinar led by Paul Offley, Compliance Officer at The Guild. The session will focus on:

  • Updates on Phase Two of the Renters’ Rights Act
  • Guidance on what agents need to know ahead of implementation
  • Answers to members’ questions
  • Continued support for navigating Phase One changes

Paul Offley emphasised the importance of staying informed: “The Renters’ Rights Act represents the most significant reform to the private rented sector in decades. While Phase Two may not require the same level of operational change as Phase One, preparing clients and understanding the upcoming requirements will be essential.”

As the private rented sector continues to evolve, property professionals may wish to take advantage of resources like this webinar to ensure they remain compliant and well-equipped to advise their landlord clients effectively.

item.title: Director dispels the top five biggest letting agent myths
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The private rented sector (PRS) has undergone significant changes this year, with the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act (RRA) and the rollout of Making Tax Digital (MTD). Amidst these developments, letting agents continue to play a crucial role in guiding landlords through the complexities of property management. However, misconceptions about their profession and value persist. Here, we explore some of the most common myths surrounding letting agents and their services.

Myth 1: Self-Management is Cheaper

One of the most prevalent myths is that landlords can save money by managing their properties themselves, avoiding letting agent fees. Whilst this may seem cost-effective on the surface, the reality is often quite different. The most significant expenses for landlords typically arise from issues such as tenant arrears, void periods, and compliance failures—not management fees. Self-management might appear cheaper when everything runs smoothly, but such scenarios are never guaranteed. Professional letting agents offer added value by reducing risks, ensuring operational efficiency, and providing peace of mind that goes beyond mere protection.

Myth 2: Finding Tenants is the Hardest Part

Another common misconception is that the most challenging aspect of being a landlord is finding tenants. Whilst tenant-finding services are widely available, securing a tenant is just the beginning, not the end of the process. Even if a tenant passes reference checks, this does not guarantee they will be reliable or trouble-free. Letting agents bring experience and judgement to tenant selection, going beyond basic reports to ensure trustworthy individuals occupy the property. Additionally, agents handle tenant deposits correctly, navigating the process efficiently and minimising the need for adjudication by the Tenancy Deposit Scheme.

Myth 3: All Letting Agent Advice is Available Online

With the wealth of information available online, some landlords believe they can bypass letting agents altogether by relying on digital resources. However, the PRS is governed by hundreds of pieces of legislation, and letting agents possess specialised expertise in navigating these regulations. Whilst online sources can provide general guidance, they cannot replicate the tailored advice and hands-on support that agents offer. Their in-depth knowledge ensures landlords remain compliant and avoid costly mistakes.

Letting agents provide invaluable support to landlords, particularly in a sector that is constantly evolving. By dispelling these myths, it becomes clear that their role extends far beyond basic property management, offering expertise and peace of mind that can save landlords time, money, and stress in the long run.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest BoE Money and Credit report
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market showed signs of modest recovery in June, with mortgage approvals for home purchases and remortgaging both increasing according to the latest Bank of England data. Industry experts suggest a combination of stable interest rates, competitive mortgage deals and easing inflation may be helping to rebuild buyer confidence, though challenges remain for both purchasers and sellers in the current climate.

Mortgage approvals show cautious improvement

The Bank of England's Money and Credit report revealed net mortgage approvals for house purchases rose to 58,200 in June, up from 56,600 the previous month. Remortgaging approvals also saw a slight increase, climbing to 34,200 from 33,800 in May. Perhaps more significantly, net mortgage borrowing more than doubled to £7.7bn compared to May's £3.3bn, comfortably exceeding the six-month average of £4.9bn.

Property professionals note these figures suggest a gradual return of market activity, though remain below recent averages. The Guild of Property Professionals' Iain McKenzie observed that while confidence is rebuilding, buyers continue to proceed carefully. With more properties available than in recent years, purchasers are taking their time and negotiating firmly on price.

Mixed economic picture influences market

Several factors appear to be influencing current market conditions. Propertymark's Nathan Emerson pointed to the stable base rate, competitive mortgage products and easing inflation as positive signs supporting buyer confidence. However, he cautioned that inflation remains above target and rising energy costs could still pressure household budgets.

The market appears to be entering a more balanced phase after an early summer slowdown. Fine & Country's Nicky Stevenson noted the current environment differs markedly from the frenetic activity of recent years, with buyers now enjoying greater choice and negotiating power. This shift means sellers may need to adjust their expectations, as properties priced realistically tend to attract interest while overpriced homes often require reductions and linger on the market.

Practical considerations for market participants

For those considering entering the market, several practical points emerge from the latest data:

  • Buyers may find more choice and negotiating room than in recent years
  • Competitive mortgage rates could make this an opportune time to secure financing
  • Sellers might need to focus on realistic pricing to attract serious interest
  • Both buyers and sellers should factor in ongoing economic uncertainties

While the figures suggest some positive momentum, the property market continues to navigate a complex economic landscape. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to stay informed about market developments and seek professional advice tailored to their individual circumstances.

item.title: Estate agent gears up for cycling challenge
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A group of estate agents from Parkers Properties is preparing to embark on a charity cycling challenge this September, aiming to raise £10,000 for Ronald McDonald House Charities in Oxford. The Tour de Parkers event will see eight cyclists, including Brendan and Lisa Kay, owners of Parkers’ Witney and Eynsham branches, pedal over 200 miles across four counties in just two days.

The Route and Purpose

Starting at the Parkers branch in Stroud on September 10, the team will cycle to all 17 Parkers offices across Oxfordshire, Berkshire, Hampshire, and Gloucestershire. The challenge will conclude at the company’s new Basingstoke office on the second day. This ambitious route highlights the group’s commitment to supporting Ronald McDonald House Oxford, which provides accommodation for families with children receiving treatment at Oxford Children’s Hospital.

Ronald McDonald House opened in April 2020 and offers a “home away from home” for families during difficult times. With 62 bedrooms, kitchens, laundry facilities, and communal spaces, the charity helps families maintain a sense of normality whilst their children undergo medical care. Chloe Hodgson, a community fundraiser for the charity, emphasised the importance of corporate partnerships, particularly during the cost-of-living crisis.

A Personal Connection

For Brendan Kay, managing director of Parkers West Oxfordshire, and his colleagues Lisa Kay and Simon Gregory, the cause holds personal significance. They have experienced the support provided by Ronald McDonald House firsthand and are passionate about giving back. This marks the second Tour de Parkers event, with the first taking place seven years ago and raising nearly £6,000 for the same charity.

The cycling team, which also includes Theo Smith, Ash Howes, Morgan Jones, Toby Phillips, and Jayson Wicks, has been training rigorously for the challenge. Their goal is to raise £10,000 to help Ronald McDonald House continue its vital work. Last year, the charity supported over 1,000 families, offering a lifeline during incredibly challenging times.

The Tour de Parkers is a testament to the power of community and corporate support for charitable causes. As the team gears up for their two-day ride, their efforts will not only raise funds but also awareness of the invaluable services provided by Ronald McDonald House Charities.

item.title: EYE NEWS UPDATE: Foxtons profits slide as sales slowdown and rental reforms bite
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Foxtons, the London-focused estate agency, has seen a significant decline in its first-half profits, driven by a slowdown in property sales and the impact of recent rental reforms. Despite a relatively stable lettings business, the group reported a 3% drop in revenue to £83.7m for the six months ending 30 June, with pre-tax profits plummeting by 57% to £4.4m. The challenging market conditions, including higher interest rates and geopolitical uncertainty, have compounded the effects of last year’s stamp duty-driven activity coming to an end.

Market Challenges Impact Sales Revenue

Foxtons’ sales revenue experienced a sharp decline of 13% during the period, reflecting lower transaction volumes across the property market. The estate agency attributed this downturn to a combination of factors, including weaker consumer confidence and the lingering effects of elevated mortgage rates. Additionally, the group noted that the uncertainty surrounding interest rate hikes and broader economic instability has deterred potential buyers, further dampening sales activity. Whilst the lettings division remained resilient, with revenue broadly flat, the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act led to a £3m reversal of previously recognised revenue due to increased tenant-led terminations.

Financial Services and Cost-Saving Measures Offer Some Relief

Amidst the challenging trading environment, Foxtons’ financial services arm provided a glimmer of hope, with revenue rising by 20%. This growth was driven by increased refinancing activity and higher ancillary income. The group also emphasised its strategic focus on diversifying income streams, with recurring and non-cyclical revenues now accounting for 69% of total revenue, up from 65% a year earlier. To mitigate the impact of reduced profitability, Foxtons implemented cost-saving measures, generating £1.3m in savings during the first half and anticipating annualised benefits of around £4.5m.

Despite these efforts, net debt increased to £28.4m, reflecting lower cash generation, acquisition spending of £8.8m, and shareholder returns. To support future growth, the group expanded its revolving credit facility from £40m to £50m. Foxtons maintained its interim dividend at 0.24p per share, signalling confidence in its long-term strategy despite ongoing market uncertainty.

Whilst the first half of the year has been challenging for Foxtons, the group believes the operational and cost actions taken have positioned it for future growth. However, with continued volatility in both the sales and lettings markets, homeowners and landlords may wish to monitor market trends closely and seek professional advice to navigate the evolving landscape.

item.title: MP campaigner against “dodgy landlords” to work with housing minister
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Labour MP Mary Kelly Foy, a prominent campaigner against exploitative landlords and housing shortages, has been appointed Parliamentary Private Secretary (PPS) to Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook. The City of Durham MP will join the Housing, Communities and Local Government team as the government prepares to launch what it describes as the largest council house building programme since the postwar era.

Campaigner takes housing role

The appointment places Foy, a member of Labour's Socialist Campaign Group, in a position to influence housing policy after years of grassroots activism. The MP has frequently highlighted issues including unaffordable rents, inadequate social housing stock, and questionable practices by some private landlords in her Durham constituency.

In a social media statement, Foy expressed enthusiasm about supporting the government's housing agenda, particularly its commitment to expand council housing provision. Housing campaigners will be watching closely to see whether her appointment leads to stronger tenant protections in the private rental sector.

Focus on student housing crisis

The Durham MP has been particularly vocal about housing challenges facing university students. In 2022, she publicly condemned the chaotic rental market in Durham after reports emerged of students queueing overnight outside letting agents to secure accommodation.

Foy described the situation - characterised by soaring rents and extreme competition for limited properties - as "ludicrous". Her intervention followed complaints from numerous students and parents about the financial and emotional strain caused by housing insecurity during their studies.

With student housing remaining a pressure point in many university towns, housing professionals suggest Foy's frontline experience could inform national policy discussions about balancing the rights of tenants, landlords and educational institutions.

What this means for housing policy

Foy's appointment comes as the new Labour government prepares its first major housing reforms. While details remain unclear, ministers have signalled priorities including:

  • Accelerating social housing construction
  • Addressing so-called "fleecehold" practices in leasehold properties
  • Tackling poor conditions in parts of the private rental sector

Property industry analysts suggest the government may introduce stronger protections for private renters while attempting to boost housing supply across all tenures. For homeowners and prospective buyers, the emphasis on new council house building could potentially ease some pressure in the broader housing market.

As the new housing team takes shape, all eyes will be on whether campaigners like Foy can translate their grassroots concerns into effective policy changes that address Britain's persistent housing challenges.

item.title: Final Section 21 deadline is on Friday
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords in England relying on pre-existing Section 21 notices have until Friday 31st July to initiate formal court proceedings, marking the final deadline under transitional arrangements following the abolition of "no-fault" evictions. The Renters' Rights Act 2025, which came into force on 1st May, eliminated Section 21 for both new and existing private tenancies, though notices served before this date were temporarily preserved.

Key dates and requirements for landlords

For a Section 21 notice to remain valid beyond this week's deadline, landlords must have submitted a formal possession claim to the court by Friday. Government guidance clarifies that preparatory actions – such as instructing solicitors, drafting paperwork, or verbally informing tenants about potential proceedings – do not satisfy this legal requirement. If court proceedings aren't commenced by the deadline, the notice becomes invalid, requiring landlords to start afresh under the reformed Section 8 process.

Some notices may have already expired under their original time limits, whilst others will become void after Friday unless court action has been initiated. Limited exceptions apply, including cases where tenants are in a formal "breathing space" debt respite scheme.

Next steps for property owners

Landlords missing the deadline will need to pursue possession through Section 8 grounds, which require demonstrating specific circumstances such as:

  • Substantial rent arrears
  • Anti-social behaviour by tenants
  • Genuine intention to sell the property
  • Planned occupation by the landlord or close family members

Each ground carries distinct notice periods and evidentiary requirements. Property professionals are advising landlords to seek urgent legal advice if they wish to act on pre-May Section 21 notices, emphasising that time is now extremely limited.

Implications for tenants and agents

Tenants who received Section 21 notices prior to May are being advised to verify whether formal court proceedings have actually commenced, rather than relying on informal communications from landlords or agents. Legal specialists note that a Section 21 notice alone doesn't compel a tenant to vacate – only a court order can do this, with bailiffs potentially involved if tenants remain after due process.

Letting agents should ensure clear communication with both landlords and tenants, avoiding any suggestion that a notice equates to an immediate eviction. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has published detailed guidance for all parties navigating these transitional arrangements.

As the property market adapts to these significant legislative changes, both landlords and tenants may wish to familiarise themselves with the new possession process under Section 8, which places greater emphasis on documented grounds for ending tenancies.

item.title: Phase 2 of Awaab’s Law puts landlords on high alert
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Social landlords across England are being urged to prepare for the second phase of Awaab’s Law, which comes into force on 30 November 2026. The expanded regulations will introduce stricter timelines for addressing additional property hazards, with industry experts warning that the winter implementation date could create immediate challenges for housing providers.

What changes under Phase 2?

Building on the initial legislation introduced in October 2025, Phase 2 of Awaab’s Law extends the existing fixed investigation and repair timescales to cover seven new hazard categories. These include excess cold and heat, fire risks, electrical hazards, structural collapse risks, fall hazards and domestic hygiene issues where they pose significant tenant safety concerns.

The established response timelines remain unchanged but will now apply to these additional hazards:

  • Emergency hazards: Investigation and safety measures required within 24 hours
  • Significant hazards: Initial investigation within 10 working days, with findings reported to tenants within 3 working days of completion and necessary repairs finished within 5 working days

Winter implementation brings added pressures

Industry specialists highlight that the late November commencement coincides with the period when housing providers typically see a surge in cold-related complaints. The UK Academy of Mould Experts (UKAME) notes that winter conditions not only increase reports of excess cold but also exacerbate condensation and mould issues - hazards already covered under Phase 1 of the legislation.

Tristan Hemsley, a disrepair and Awaab’s Law consultant, explains: "Unlike the initial implementation, landlords won't have a gradual adjustment period. The expanded rules take effect at the peak season for several of these hazards, meaning compliant responses will be immediately tested."

Hemsley cites the example of boiler failures reported from 30 November onwards, which may require emergency response within 24 hours - particularly for vulnerable residents. This underscores the need for robust winter preparedness from housing providers.

Preparation key for compliance

With four months until implementation, social landlords might consider reviewing several operational areas:

  • Updating reporting systems to properly categorise the new hazard types
  • Reviewing contractor agreements to ensure capacity for prompt response
  • Training staff across all relevant departments on the expanded requirements
  • Developing clear escalation protocols for the additional hazard categories

As the sector adapts to these wider responsibilities, the coming months present a critical window for housing providers to strengthen their compliance frameworks before the winter deadline.

item.title: Eight renters are chasing every available property
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK rental market continues to face significant challenges, with demand far outstripping supply, according to the latest data from Propertymark, the trade body for letting agents. The figures for May reveal that an average of eight prospective tenants are competing for each available rental property, highlighting the ongoing housing shortage in the private rented sector.

Rental Market Strain

Propertymark’s report shows that the average letting agent branch had just over 12 properties available to rent in May, a slight decrease from previous months. Meanwhile, tenant registrations surged to an average of 98 per branch, indicating strong demand. New property instructions also declined, with an average of just 2.39 fully managed properties added per branch during the month.

Nathan Emerson, Chief Executive of Propertymark, commented on the persistent imbalance between supply and demand. “Although tenant demand increased in May, available stock fell slightly, leaving an average of eight applicants chasing every available property,” he said. Emerson also warned that ongoing legislative changes and financial pressures on landlords could further limit investment in the private rented sector, exacerbating the shortage of homes.

Challenges for Tenants and Landlords

Phil Spencer, founder of Move iQ, echoed these concerns, noting that securing a suitable rental property remains a significant challenge for tenants. “With only around 12 properties available per letting branch and demand continuing to outstrip supply, many tenants are facing limited choice and strong competition,” he said. While rent increases appear to be stabilising in some areas, the underlying shortage of rental homes means tenants often find themselves in competitive situations whenever a property becomes available.

Rental arrears have eased marginally, but the broader pressures on the sector remain. Landlords are grappling with rising costs and regulatory changes, which may deter future investment in rental properties. This could further tighten supply, leaving tenants with even fewer options.

Sales Market Trends

Propertymark’s report also provided insights into the sales market. The average branch agreed eight sales during May, consistent with April’s figures. However, new prospective buyer registrations dropped to 64 per branch, suggesting a potential cooling in buyer demand. On a positive note, the number of available properties increased slightly to 44 per branch.

Despite this, 84% of agents reported that properties were selling below their asking price, with only 11% achieving the full asking price. Branches received an average of 10.1 new sales instructions and conducted 20 market appraisals during the month. Properties attracted an average of 2.2 viewings, unchanged from April.

As the housing market continues to evolve, both renters and buyers face challenges in finding suitable properties. With supply struggling to keep pace with demand, stakeholders may need to explore innovative solutions to address the ongoing imbalance.

item.title: 4% fall in new home registrations
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market has faced fresh challenges, with new home registrations declining by 4% in the second quarter of 2026, according to recent data. The National House Building Council (NHBC) has highlighted significant regional disparities in this trend, whilst also expressing optimism about potential growth in council house building initiatives.

Regional disparities in new home registrations

The NHBC report reveals that the drop in new home registrations was not uniform across the country. Some regions experienced sharper declines compared to others, reflecting varying levels of demand and construction activity. For instance, areas with higher property prices and limited land availability saw more pronounced reductions, whilst regions with more affordable housing markets fared slightly better.

This disparity underscores the complexity of the UK housing market, where local factors such as planning permissions, land availability, and economic conditions play a crucial role in shaping housing supply. Homebuilders and policymakers may need to address these regional imbalances to ensure a more consistent flow of new homes nationwide.

The role of council house building

Amidst the decline in new home registrations, there is growing hope that increased council house building could help alleviate the housing shortage. The NHBC has pointed to the potential for local authorities to play a more active role in delivering affordable housing, particularly in areas where private developers are facing challenges.

Council house building programmes could provide a much-needed boost to the housing market, offering affordable options for first-time buyers and families struggling to enter the property ladder. However, the success of such initiatives will depend on adequate funding, streamlined planning processes, and collaboration between local councils and housing associations.

As the UK navigates these challenges, it will be important to monitor how regional disparities and council house building efforts evolve in the coming months. Addressing these issues could help create a more balanced and sustainable housing market for the future.

item.title: Developer confidence dives
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK property developers are adopting a more cautious approach to new projects as rising construction costs and lengthy planning processes dampen market confidence. Industry reports suggest this growing wariness is leading many developers to explore specialist financing options to navigate the challenging conditions.

Construction costs and delays impact developer sentiment

Several factors appear to be contributing to the decline in developer confidence. Build costs have risen significantly across materials and labour, squeezing profit margins on new developments. Meanwhile, planning departments continue to face backlogs, with many applications taking considerably longer than the statutory timeframe to receive approval.

These challenges are particularly affecting:

  • Small and medium-sized developers with limited financial buffers
  • Projects in areas with particularly stretched local authority resources
  • Schemes requiring complex planning permissions

Specialist finance options gaining traction

With traditional development finance becoming harder to secure for some projects, many developers are turning to alternative funding solutions. Specialist lenders are reporting increased interest in products designed to address current market conditions, including:

  • Bridging loans with extended terms
  • Development exit finance
  • Mezzanine financing options

These products can provide developers with greater flexibility during the construction phase and help bridge funding gaps caused by delays. However, borrowers might consider that specialist finance typically comes with higher interest rates and fees compared to conventional development loans.

While the current climate presents challenges for developers, the underlying demand for new housing remains strong. Those navigating the market may wish to explore all financing options and build contingency plans to account for potential delays and cost increases.

item.title: Semi-commercial lending to hit £1bn
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK’s semi-commercial lending market is experiencing significant growth, with forecasts suggesting it could exceed £1 billion by 2026. This surge is driven by expanding specialist lenders and increasing investor interest in mixed-use properties, which combine residential and commercial elements. Such properties are becoming a popular choice for those looking to diversify their portfolios or maximise rental income.

What is Semi-Commercial Lending?

Semi-commercial lending refers to mortgages designed for properties that serve both residential and commercial purposes. These could include buildings with shops on the ground floor and flats above, or offices with attached living spaces. Unlike purely residential mortgages, semi-commercial loans cater to the unique needs of mixed-use properties, often requiring different criteria and terms.

Specialist lenders have been at the forefront of this market, offering tailored solutions that traditional high-street banks may not provide. Their flexibility and understanding of mixed-use properties have made them increasingly attractive to investors.

Why is Demand Growing?

Several factors are contributing to the rising demand for semi-commercial lending. Mixed-use properties often offer higher rental yields compared to purely residential or commercial buildings, making them an appealing option for investors. Additionally, these properties can provide a hedge against market volatility, as they are less reliant on a single sector.

  • Diversification: Mixed-use properties allow investors to spread risk across residential and commercial tenants.
  • Location Benefits: Many mixed-use properties are situated in prime urban areas, attracting both businesses and residents.
  • Flexibility: The dual-purpose nature of these properties can adapt to changing market conditions.

The Role of Specialist Lenders

Specialist lenders have played a crucial role in the growth of semi-commercial lending. They often provide more flexible terms and a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in mixed-use properties. This has made them a go-to option for investors seeking financing outside the traditional banking sector.

As the market evolves, these lenders are expected to continue innovating, offering products that cater to the unique needs of mixed-use property investors. This, in turn, is likely to drive further growth in the sector.

With semi-commercial lending on track to reach £1 billion by 2026, the market is set to play an increasingly important role in the UK’s property landscape. Borrowers might consider exploring this option if they are looking to invest in mixed-use properties, whilst keeping in mind the potential complexities and benefits involved.

item.title: Pack your bucket and spade
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Beach hut prices across the UK have seen a second consecutive annual decline, potentially offering prospective buyers more affordable opportunities to own a slice of coastal charm. With values softening in several sought-after seaside spots, those considering a beachside investment or holiday retreat may find improved market conditions this summer.

Why beach hut prices are falling

Industry analysts suggest several factors have contributed to the recent price dip in beach hut markets. Whilst these colourful cabins remain highly desirable, changing holiday patterns post-pandemic and rising maintenance costs have cooled demand slightly in certain locations. Additionally, some coastal councils have introduced stricter regulations around hut usage, affecting their appeal to some buyers.

Popular spots like Bournemouth, Brighton and Whitstable continue to command premium prices, but even these areas have experienced modest price corrections. More affordable options can often be found in emerging coastal towns where regeneration projects are enhancing local amenities whilst keeping prices relatively low.

What prospective buyers should consider

Those interested in purchasing a beach hut might want to research several key aspects before committing:

  • Local council regulations regarding usage, subletting and alterations
  • Annual maintenance costs and service charges
  • Accessibility and parking facilities
  • Length of the letting season in the chosen location
  • Insurance requirements and costs

Whilst beach huts rarely offer residential accommodation, they can provide enjoyable holiday escapes and potential rental income opportunities during peak seasons. However, buyers should be aware that these properties typically require cash purchases, as mortgage finance is rarely available for such unconventional dwellings.

For those drawn to coastal living, the current market conditions might present a favourable window to secure a beach hut at more accessible price points than seen in recent years. As always with property purchases, thorough research and professional advice are recommended before proceeding with any transaction.

item.title: HMRC nets £104m in voluntary disclosures
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Revenue & Customs has collected £104 million from private landlords who voluntarily disclosed unpaid taxes on rental income, signalling heightened enforcement activity in the property sector. The substantial sum recovered through voluntary disclosures suggests many buy-to-let investors may have previously underreported earnings, with tax authorities now intensifying scrutiny of rental portfolios.

Growing pressure on landlords' tax compliance

Property investors face increasing obligations to accurately declare all rental profits following HMRC's expanded compliance initiatives. The tax authority has significantly boosted its property income campaign in recent years, using sophisticated data-matching technology to cross-reference landlord records with tenancy agreements, mortgage applications and deposit protection schemes.

Landlords might consider reviewing their tax positions carefully, as HMRC can investigate returns going back up to 20 years in cases of deliberate tax avoidance. Common areas of underpayment include failing to declare:

  • Rental income from lodgers or multiple properties
  • Capital gains from property sales
  • Overseas rental earnings
  • Benefit-in-kind from rent-free arrangements

Voluntary disclosure options available

Property owners who identify discrepancies in their tax affairs may benefit from coming forward proactively through HMRC's Let Property Campaign. This voluntary disclosure scheme typically results in lower penalties than cases where HMRC initiates investigations, with fines potentially reduced by up to 30% for full cooperation.

The campaign allows landlords to:

  • Calculate unpaid tax using simplified forms
  • Disclose omissions from previous years
  • Arrange manageable repayment plans
  • Receive certainty about their tax position

With HMRC increasingly collaborating with lettings agencies and property platforms to identify non-compliance, buy-to-let investors may wish to ensure their records are complete and up-to-date. Professional tax advice could prove valuable for those with complex property holdings or uncertainty about their obligations.
